newsitem.title: RUSSIA: IMF may offer Russia words, not cash, in near term.
newsitem.headline: IMF may offer Russia words, not cash, in near term.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund, assessing Russia's ability to improve a dismal record on tax collection, may offer words of support after November economic checks, but economists said IMF purse strings could stay shut.

The IMF has already delayed handing over one tranche of a $10 billion three-year loan to Russia. Officials say they want evidence of a sustainable improvement in tax collection before they will unlock the funds.

"If the IMF says nice things about the country but waits another couple of weeks to see if the current increase in tax revenues continues, it's not going to be particularly negative," said Roland Nash, chief economist at Renaissance Capital.
"The important thing is that the Russian government can prove that they have increased tax (collection) rates from the previous months and that they will keep things at these levels."
A second economist said: "It might take a little bit longer for the IMF to decide how well Russia is really doing."

Russian tax revenues improved sharply last month and officials highlighted this in interviews and press comments before the IMF's latest monitoring mission arrived. The mission is likely to be in Moscow until late next week.
But some officials hinted that failure to release delayed funds would not be an economic tragedy.

"We do not have to be obsessed with receiving the $340 million," Central Bank chief Sergei Dubinin told Sevodnya newspaper this week, referring to the October tranche. "What is important is economic policy."

Policy has been aimed at squeezing inflation out of the economy, although tight monetary policies and low tax revenues have hurt many in the hard-pressed Russian economy, where millions of workers have not been paid for months.

The government, which has set up an emergency commission to force tax debtors to pay, blames companies who do not pay their bills. The firms say they cannot pay because their clients -- including the government and the state sector -- owe them cash.
Most officials say the broad outline of policy will remain unchanged despite the cash crunch and the social hardships the wage arrears have brought.
But the minister in charge of social policy said on Thursday that Russia might have to risk annoying the IMF to pay millions of dollars in overdue pensions.

"The situation with debts for pensions is so serious that it seems we may have to go ahead with a decision that might not please certain international monetary organisations," First Deputy Prime Minister Viktor Ilyushin said.
It was not clear if this represented a new official policy.
Official figures show Russian wage arrears totalled over 43 trillion roubles ($7.8 billion) last month, forming one of the bleakest images in a mixed economic picture.
The economy has not recovered from a prolonged slump and the fall in gross domestic product doubled to six percent in the first 10 months of 1996, from three percent in the first 10 months of 1995.

But year-on-year inflation, forced down by tight monetary policies, is at its lowest level since economic reforms began in January 1992. News that Japan was releasing a long-frozen $500 million loan programme will also be welcome news.
Japanese officials said on Friday the bulk of the aid package would be commercial and industrial projects in the form of loans from Japan's Export-Import Bank.

Whether the IMF releases its cash or not, Russia will get some finance from its first post-tsarist sovereign eurobond and officials are outlining the state of the Russian economy at a roadshow in major financial centres this month.
The roadshow started in Tokyo on Monday and ends in the United States next week.
($1=5489 Rouble)
